Fanny Pack
FAN-ee pak
noun (Gen X slang)
American, from fanny, informal US English for the backside (early 20th century), and pack. Belt pouches had long served skiers, hikers, and cyclists; the zippered nylon fanny pack became a mass fashion item in the mid-to-late 1980s, the uniform of tourists, theme-park parents, and mall walkers, and a byword for unfashionable practicality by the late 1990s. In Britain it is called a bum bag, since fanny is impolite there. It returned in the 2010s as the belt bag.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The fanny pack was the 1980s answer to a simple problem: where do you keep your wallet, keys, sunscreen, and gum when you are walking all day? Strap a zippered pouch around your waist and your hands are free and your treasure is right in front of you. By the 1990s it was the punchline of every tourist joke. The Christian observation is that the Bible has a good deal to say about bags. David went out to meet Goliath with five smooth stones in "a shepherd’s bag which he had, even in a scrip" (1Sa 17:40) — a waist pouch carrying a great faith. Jesus sent out the seventy with orders to "Carry neither purse, nor scrip, nor shoes" (Luk 10:4), so they would learn the Father provides. Haggai describes the frustrated worker who "earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes" (Hag 1:6) — money that leaks away because God is not first. And the Lord commands a different kind of pack entirely: "provide yourselves bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not" (Luk 12:33). The fanny pack keeps valuables close and in sight, which is exactly the instinct Jesus redirects: "where your treasure is, there will your heart be also" (Mat 6:21). A father can laugh at the photo of himself at the theme park in 1989 with a neon pouch around his middle; then he can ask his children what they keep closest, and whether it is the kind of bag that waxes old.

Webster 1828 Definition

American name (from fanny, the backside) for the zippered waist pouch of the mid-to-late 1980s, the tourist’s uniform and later a fashion joke; Scripture asks what we carry close, and bids us provide bags which wax not old (Luk 12:33).

FANNY PACK, n. (Gen X slang, American; mass fashion mid-to-late 1980s) A small zippered pouch worn on a belt around the waist, for keys, money, and snacks. "The tickets are in my fanny pack."

From US informal fanny, the backside, + pack; British bum bag, since fanny is impolite there.

Earlier a skier’s and hiker’s belt pouch; revived in the 2010s as the belt bag or sling.

Webster 1828: PACK, n. [See the Verb.] 1. A bundle of any thing inclosed in a cover or bound fast with cords; a bale; as a pack of goods or cloth. The soldier bears a pack on his back. 2. A burden or load; as a pack of sorrows. …

Decode for parents: the fanny pack keeps treasure close; ask your children what treasure they keep closest.

Key Scripture

1Sa 17:40 — "And he took his staff in his hand, and chose him five smooth stones out of the brook, and put them in a shepherd's bag which he had, even in a scrip; and his sling was in his hand: and he drew near to the Philistine."

Luk 10:4 — "Carry neither purse, nor scrip, nor shoes: and salute no man by the way."

Hag 1:6 — "Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes."

Luk 12:33 — "Sell that ye have, and give alms; provide yourselves bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not, where no thief approacheth, neither moth corrupteth."

Mat 6:21 — "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also."

Modern Corruption

The fanny pack is a harmless convenience that became a fashion joke; Scripture uses bags and purses to ask the deeper question — what treasure we keep close, and whether the bag has holes.

expand to see more

The bag with holes. Haggai’s people worked hard and stayed poor; their wages went into "a bag with holes" (Hag 1:6) because they built their own houses and left God’s in ruins. The 1980s were a decade of earning and spending, and many Gen X children watched parents strap on the pouch for one more trip to one more mall. The fanny pack is innocent; the anxious grip on what is inside it is the thing worth examining. Treasure laid up on earth, Jesus warned, is subject to moth, rust, and thieves.

Traveling light. Jesus sent His disciples out without purse or scrip (Luk 10:4), and when He asked afterward whether they had lacked anything, they said, Nothing. The lesson was not that Christians must never carry a wallet — He later told them to take one — but that the Father provides. David’s scrip held five stones and a great faith (1Sa 17:40). The Christian’s best pack is the one Christ commands: bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not (Luk 12:33).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Middle Dutch pak → English pack; US informal fanny (the backside) → 1980s fanny pack (British bum bag) → 2010s belt bag; Scripture: bags which wax not old (Luk 12:33).

expand to see more

Middle Dutch pak → Middle English pakke — a bundle, a load to be carried

Early 20th-c. US informal fanny — the backside

1970s: belt pouches for skiers and hikers; mid-to-late 1980s: mass fashion

1990s: the tourist’s uniform and a fashion punchline; 2010s revival as the belt bag

Biblical bags: David’s scrip (1Sa 17:40); the bag with holes (Hag 1:6); bags which wax not old (Luk 12:33)
